problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$
worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $(-3,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
